title: Why the First Buyers of a New Tower Pay Less: Off-Plan Pricing Explained
seoTitle: Why First Buyers of a New Tower Pay Less (Off-Plan)
description: The first buyers in a presale get the lowest price, but it is not a gift. Learn why banks push developers to presell and why that early price disappears.
answer: The first buyers of a new tower pay less because they carry the most risk. Before a developer can build, the bank wants proof of demand, so the developer sells a large share of the building on paper first, often 30 to 50 percent. Nothing is built and nothing is certain yet. The low price is payment for going first, and it is gone once the crane goes up.
body:
Many people think the first buyers in a new tower got lucky, or that the developer is being generous. Neither is true. The early price is low for a very specific reason, and once you understand it, you understand how off-plan pricing works.

## Why the bank decides when a tower gets built

A developer rarely builds a tower with only their own money. They need a construction loan, and the bank does not lend on a nice idea. The bank wants proof that real people want to live in this building or own a unit in it.

So before construction starts, the developer has to sell a big part of the building on paper. In many projects that is 30 to 50 percent of the units. Those early contracts are the evidence the bank needs to release the money.

## What the first buyers are really buying

At that moment, the first buyers are signing for something that does not exist yet. There is no structure, no finished lobby and no completion date that anyone can guarantee. They are taking on the most uncertainty of anyone who will ever buy in that building.

That is why they get the lowest price. It is not a discount. In my view, the right way to see it is this: **you are being paid to go first.** The lower price is compensation for the risk you carry so that the project can happen at all.

## Why the early price disappears

The price is tied to the risk. As the risk goes down, the price goes up. The clearest signal is the crane. Once the bank has released the loan and construction starts, the project is far more certain than it was on paper.

The buyers who come after that point carry less risk, so they pay more. The day the crane goes up, the first-buyer price is gone for good.

## Price is the wrong question, timing is the right one

When people look at a presale, they usually ask whether the price is good. I think the better question is about timing:

1. How early in the project am I buying?
2. How much risk am I taking on at this stage?
3. Am I comfortable carrying that risk until construction starts?

If you buy early, you accept more uncertainty in exchange for a lower price. If you wait, you pay more for more certainty. Neither choice is wrong. What matters is knowing which trade you are making. This is my opinion and general education, not financial advice.
takeaways: Banks usually want proof of demand before they fund construction of a new tower.
Developers often presell 30 to 50 percent of a building on paper to get that proof.
The first buyers carry the most risk because nothing is built or certain yet.
The low early price is payment for going first, not a gift or a discount.
Once construction starts and the crane goes up, the first-buyer price is gone.
faq: Pre-construction prices are lower because early buyers take on the most risk. The building does not exist yet, and the developer needs their contracts to prove demand to the bank.
How many units must be presold before construction starts?
It depends on the lender and the project, but developers often sell 30 to 50 percent of the units on paper before the bank releases the construction loan.
Is buying off-plan early a good idea?
It can be, if you understand and accept the risk. You get the lowest price in exchange for uncertainty, so check the developer and the project carefully before you sign.
When do presale prices go up?
Prices usually rise as risk falls. The biggest step is when construction starts, because the project becomes far more certain than it was on paper.
